profiles.summary: Bor runs the Prague instruction set plus CLZ, with Polygon-only changes to storage gas, code size and the transaction gas cap. Every opcode the PoolManager bytecode needs is present.

deltas.delta: Chicago fork (mainnet block 87218600) applies PIP-88. Cold SLOAD costs 5460 gas where Ethereum charges 2100, and the cold SSTORE surcharge is 2940. Swaps that cross many ticks cost more gas than on Ethereum.
Maximum contract code size is 32768 bytes since Ahmedabad (PIP-30). Ethereum allows 24576. Hooks can be larger. The PoolManager is unaffected.
EIP-7702 set-code transactions are live since Bhilai, as on Ethereum. A hook address can be a delegated account whose code target changes.
Lisovo adds the CLZ opcode. An eth_call that executes opcode 0x1e returned a result. The PoolManager bytecode does not use it.
Blob opcodes are commented out of the Cancun instruction set in Bor. The PoolManager does not use them.

profiles.summary: State sync records from Ethereum run as system calls at the end of sprint-end blocks, outside user transactions. Since the Austin fork Bor resets transient storage before each record. Before Austin it did not.

deltas.delta: Bor executes each state sync record in Finalize by calling the StateReceiver at 0x1001 from system address 0xffffFFFfFFffffffffffffffFfFFFfffFFFfFFfE with zero gas price. The call does not go through the normal transaction path.

PrepareStateSyncContext calls StateDB.Prepare before each record once the Austin fork is active (mainnet block 91949700). Prepare replaces the transient storage map. For blocks before Austin the function returns without doing anything, and no other code on that path resets transient storage. In the v2.11.0 source this means transient storage written by the last user transaction of a pre-Austin block stays readable during state sync execution.
Any Ethereum account can make a state sync call reach an arbitrary Polygon contract through FxPortal. FxChild.onStateReceive forwards to processMessageFromRoot on a receiver named in the message.
Since Madhugiri (PIP-74) a block that ran state syncs carries one type 0x7F transaction with from and to set to the zero address. It executes no EVM code and changes no state.
Bor executes blocks with BlockSTM. Release v2.11.0 bounds speculative work per block and falls back to serial execution when the bound is hit.

findings.title: Scheduled Jenner fork adds protocol-native tokens whose issuer can seize, pause or block the PoolManager balance
findings.difference: BNB Smart Chain has scheduled the Jenner fork for 2026-12-08 02:30 UTC. It ships BEP-702, a token standard named CAS20 that runs as native code behind addresses starting with 0xCA52. Every CAS20 token has a role that can reassign a holder's balance (seizeWithMemo), a per-feature pause, and transfer policies that read shared allowlists and blocklists. BEP-703 lets governance list these tokens as payment assets with reserved block space. Ethereum has no token logic in the protocol.
findings.mechanism: 1. The PoolManager keeps every pool's reserves, all ERC-6909 claims and accrued protocol fees for a currency in one balance, read by balanceOf at src/types/Currency.sol:94 and paid out by transfer at src/types/Currency.sol:60-75. 2. A CAS20 token keeps the transfer and balanceOf selectors, so pools can be initialized with it. initialize makes no call to the currency (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142). 3. The token admin points SEIZE_HOLDER_POLICY at a blocklist that contains the PoolManager address. An account with SEIZE_ROLE then calls seizeWithMemo(PoolManager, to, value). The balance moves without any take, and no delta is recorded. Pool accounting still shows the old reserves, so the last liquidity providers and claim holders to exit find transfer failing for lack of balance. 4. If TRANSFER_SENDER_POLICY stops authorizing the PoolManager, or the TRANSFER feature is paused, the token reverts every transfer from the PoolManager. Currency.transfer then reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86, so take (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56) fail for every pool that uses the token. 5. If TRANSFER_RECEIVER_POLICY stops authorizing the PoolManager, nobody can pay the token in, and settle credits nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). 6. The Asset variant multiplier does not change balanceOf, so it creates no rebase at the PoolManager. That part was checked and is safe.
findings.impact: All reserves, ERC-6909 claims and protocol fees held in the affected CAS20 token across every pool. Seizure is a loss for liquidity providers of those pools. A policy change or pause is a freeze that lasts until the issuer reverses it. Liquidity providers can still remove liquidity, take the counter-asset and hold the affected token as an ERC-6909 claim through mint (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), because mint makes no token call.
findings.preconditions: Jenner activates as scheduled, chain governance opens CAS20 creation through the ActivationRegistry, a CAS20 token is created, and pools holding it exist on the PoolManager. The issuer roles of that token must then act. An unprivileged attacker can do this only with a token it issued itself, which harms only those who pool against that token. None of these conditions hold today. The factory and registry addresses have no code at the time of the query. The BEP is still marked Draft and the client implementation was not read, so the final behaviour could differ from the text.
findings.mitigations: Treat CAS20 tokens as issuer-controlled assets in interfaces and routing. Before listing a CAS20 pool, read the token's six policy ids, its pause mask and the holders of SEIZE_ROLE and the admin role. Prefer tokens whose role membership is frozen with no seizer. Liquidity providers should size positions on the assumption that the issuer can take or freeze the pooled balance. After the fork, re-test take and settle against a CAS20 token on a fork node.

findings.title: Polygon system token at 0x1010 mirrors the PoolManager native balance and cannot be paid out by take
findings.difference: Polygon has a genesis contract at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 that presents native POL as a token. Its balanceOf returns the native balance of the account. Its transfer is payable and returns false unless msg.value equals the amount. Ethereum has no ERC-20 face of ETH at the protocol level.
findings.mechanism: 1. sync(0x1010) stores balanceOf(PoolManager) as reserves (src/PoolManager.sol:285-286, src/types/Currency.sol:94). That value is the full native POL balance of the PoolManager, which already backs pools that use address(0). 2. settle with 0x1010 synced credits the caller with any rise in that native balance since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). msg.value is rejected at src/PoolManager.sol:356 and the PoolManager has no receive function, so the balance can rise only through a forced transfer such as SELFDESTRUCT. 3. take(0x1010, to, amount) calls transfer on 0x1010 with zero value (src/types/Currency.sol:73). The token returns a 32 byte zero. The success test at src/types/Currency.sol:68 fails and the call reverts at src/types/Currency.sol:82-86. collectProtocolFees for this currency reverts the same way (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56). 4. A positive delta in currency 0x1010 can therefore only be cleared, minted as an ERC-6909 claim, or swapped. The POL that paid for it stays in the PoolManager native balance and no account holds a native delta to take it. 5. Double credit was checked and is not possible. A native settle while 0x1010 is synced reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:356, and sync(address(0)) clears the synced currency (src/PoolManager.sol:281-283), so one POL is never credited under both currencies.
findings.impact: POL that a contract pays into a pool or claim denominated in 0x1010 cannot leave the PoolManager as that currency and is not claimable as native POL either. Pools that hold POL under address(0) are not affected. The PoolManager held about 3.1 million native POL at the time of the query. Protocol fees accrued in currency 0x1010 would also be stuck.
findings.preconditions: Someone initializes a pool with 0x1010 as a currency, and a custom contract forces POL into the PoolManager between sync and settle. Standard periphery cannot do this because approve and transferFrom on 0x1010 revert. The actor loses its own funds. No path was found that takes funds from other users.
findings.mitigations: Interfaces, routers and pool indexers on Polygon should refuse 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 as a pool currency and direct users to address(0) or WPOL. Block explorers label 0x1010 as the POL token, so the warning should be explicit in deployment notes.

findings.title: Thirteen Wormhole guardians can act as PoolManager owner on BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche
findings.difference: On Ethereum the owner is the governance timelock itself. On BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche the owner is a Uniswap Wormhole message receiver contract. It executes calls carried in a Wormhole message whose emitter is the Uniswap sender contract on Ethereum. A Wormhole message is valid with 13 of 19 guardian signatures, so the guardian set is a second party that can produce owner calls.
findings.mechanism: 1. owner() of the PoolManager is 0x341c1511141022cf8ee20824ae0ffa3491f1302b on BNB Smart Chain and 0x47eb0cf11a1626462da3c830bcde64c3f582b5a6 on Avalanche. Both contracts carry the strings 'Uniswap Wormhole Message Receiver', 'Invalid Emitter Address!' and 'Sub-call failed', and messageSender() returns 0xf5f4496219f31cdcba6130b5402873624585615a. 2. A message that passes the receiver's checks makes it call arbitrary targets. As owner it can call setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). 3. The controller can set a protocol fee on any pool up to 1000 pips per direction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32) and can withdraw accrued protocol fees to any recipient (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). The withdrawal is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued through a checked subtraction at src/ProtocolFees.sol:55. 4. On BNB Smart Chain the receiver is also owner and feeSetter of the current fee adapter. On Avalanche no controller is set, so the first message through this path would name one. 5. No owner or controller function in src/ reaches pool reserves or ERC-6909 claims. The Owned base contract comes from lib/solmate, which is an empty directory in this checkout, so its transfer function was not read.
findings.impact: Accrued protocol fees and future protocol fees of at most 0.1% of swap input per direction on every pool of the chain. Swappers pay the fee. Liquidity provider principal is not reachable through this path.
findings.preconditions: Thirteen of nineteen Wormhole guardians sign a message that Ethereum governance did not send, or the Wormhole core contract on the chain is compromised. How the receiver verifies signatures, sequence numbers and the 172800 second timeout was inferred from bytecode strings and getters. The receiver source was not read.
findings.mitigations: Monitor ProtocolFeeControllerUpdated and ProtocolFeeUpdated events on both chains and compare them with executed Ethereum governance proposals. Keep accrued protocol fees low by collecting often. Governance can move ownership to a receiver with a second independent attestation if the fee stream grows.

findings.title: Polygon state sync path lets the Heimdall validator set act as PoolManager owner
findings.difference: On Polygon the PoolManager owner is a proxy that trusts FxChild to report the Ethereum sender of a message. FxChild trusts the StateReceiver at 0x1001, and Bor calls the StateReceiver from a system address with records that Heimdall validators attest. Ethereum has no system caller that can stand in for the timelock.
findings.mechanism: 1. owner() of the PoolManager is 0x8a1b966ac46f42275860f905dbc75efbfdc12374. Its fxChild() is 0x8397259c983751daf40400790063935a11afa28a and its l1Owner() is the Ethereum timelock 0x1a9c8182c09f50c8318d769245bea52c32be35bc. 2. FxChild.onStateReceive requires msg.sender to be 0x1001, decodes the root sender and receiver from the record data and calls processMessageFromRoot on the receiver. 3. Bor delivers records in Finalize through a system call from 0xffffFFFfFFffffffffffffffFfFFFfffFFFfFFfE to 0x1001. The records come from Heimdall. 4. A record whose data names the timelock as root sender makes the proxy execute arbitrary calls as PoolManager owner. It can call setProtocolFeeController (src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). The controller then sets fees up to 1000 pips per direction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32) and withdraws accrued fees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57). The same proxy is owner and feeSetter of the current fee adapter. 5. The code at 0x1001 is itself replaced by hard forks. Uburu did so on 2026-11-05 through a release that validators ran before the source was public.
findings.impact: Accrued protocol fees (536 POL, 134 USDC and 0.03 WETH at the time of the query, among others) and future protocol fees of at most 0.1% of swap input per direction. Liquidity provider principal is not reachable through owner or controller functions in src/.
findings.preconditions: A Heimdall majority attests a state sync record that Ethereum did not emit, or a client release changes the StateReceiver or the system call path. The share of Heimdall stake needed was not confirmed from a source and is assumed to be two thirds. The proxy source and the post-Uburu StateReceiver code were not read. The proxy checks were inferred from its three selectors and its revert strings.
findings.mitigations: Monitor ProtocolFeeControllerUpdated and ProtocolFeeUpdated on Polygon against executed Ethereum proposals. Review each Bor release that touches 0x1001 or state sync execution. Collect protocol fees often so little sits in the PoolManager.

cleared.check: Whether transient storage of the PoolManager (lock flag, deltas, synced currency and reserves) can leak from the last user transaction of a block into state sync calls that an attacker reaches through FxPortal.
cleared.result: Safe since the Austin fork at mainnet block 91949700. PrepareStateSyncContext calls StateDB.Prepare before every record, and Prepare replaces the transient storage map. Before Austin the reset was missing. Even then only a stale synced currency and reserves could survive, because unlock relocks at src/PoolManager.sol:113 and requires a zero delta count at src/PoolManager.sol:112. A stale sync credits only balance that arrives after it (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360), and no third-party token flow into the PoolManager happens between the last transaction and state sync.

cleared.check: Whether Parlia system transactions run with transient storage left over from the previous transaction.
cleared.result: Safe. applyMessage calls state.Prepare for system messages once Cancun is active. System contracts do not call arbitrary contracts, so they would not reach the PoolManager in any case.

cleared.check: Whether PUSH0, TSTORE, TLOAD, MCOPY and SELFBALANCE exist on each chain (A10).
cleared.result: Safe. An eth_call contract creation that runs all five opcodes returned 32 bytes on each chain.
cleared.source: rpc eth_call with data 0x5f5f5d5f5c5060205f5f5e475f5260205ff3 on the three RPC URLs in networks.json, 2026-11-22

cleared.check: Whether one POL can be credited twice, once as address(0) and once as the 0x1010 token (A3 siphon).
cleared.result: Safe. settle rejects msg.value while a non-native currency is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356). sync(address(0)) clears the synced currency (src/PoolManager.sol:281-283), and a later sync(0x1010) records the balance that already includes the native payment. The PoolManager has no receive function, and an eth_call that sends 1 wei with empty calldata reverts. A take of native POL between sync(0x1010) and settle makes the subtraction at src/PoolManager.sol:360 revert.

cleared.check: Whether PIP-88 storage repricing together with the transaction gas cap can make a swap or a liquidity removal impossible to include (A9).
cleared.result: Safe. Cold SLOAD costs 5460 gas, and the per transaction cap is 2^25 gas, twice the Ethereum cap. A swap stops at the caller's price limit (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344), so large swaps can be split. modifyLiquidity touches a bounded number of slots.

cleared.check: Whether the BEP-652 transaction gas cap or the BEP-703 payment lane can block PoolManager operations (A9).
cleared.result: Safe. The cap is 2^24 gas, equal to Ethereum since EIP-7825. The payment lane withholds at most 10% of an 80 million gas block from general transactions.

cleared.check: Whether charging max(gasUsed, gasLimit / 2) and counting gas limits toward block size can freeze liquidity (A9).
cleared.result: Safe. It raises the cost of over-estimated gas limits. The block gas limit is 80,000,000 and no opcode price changed. Whether a per transaction cap below the block limit exists was not confirmed.

cleared.check: Whether an atomic import that credits AVAX to the PoolManager address outside the EVM gives anyone a delta (A2, A3).
cleared.result: Safe. Native payments are credited from msg.value only (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354). A balance increase that arrives without a call is credited to nobody and cannot be taken. An export needs a signature from the debited address, which a contract cannot produce. The export signature rule was not read in source.

cleared.check: Whether any caller can have msg.sender equal to address(0), the value of protocolFeeController on Avalanche, and so pass the checks at src/ProtocolFees.sol:36 and src/ProtocolFees.sol:48.
cleared.result: Safe as far as documented. The C-Chain accepts only signed legacy, EIP-2930 and EIP-1559 transactions, and atomic transactions do not run EVM code. No system call with a zero caller is documented. The new VM source was not read, so this rests on documentation.

cleared.check: Whether the PIP-74 StateSyncTx, whose from field is the zero address, can call contracts with msg.sender zero.
cleared.result: Safe. PIP-74 states the transaction executes no EVM code and changes no state. State sync calls use the system address 0xffff…fffe as caller.

cleared.check: Whether permissionless fee collection through the fee adapter while the PoolManager is unlocked lets a caller gain funds. collectProtocolFees has no lock check in this code (src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57), and _isUnlocked declared at src/ProtocolFees.sol:60 is never called there.
cleared.result: No gain found. The recipient is the adapter's token jar. The amount is bounded by protocolFeesAccrued through a checked subtraction (src/ProtocolFees.sol:55). The synced currency guard at src/ProtocolFees.sol:49 blocks collection of an ERC-20 between sync and settle. Native settle uses msg.value, so a falling native balance does not change credit. On Polygon, collecting native fees while 0x1010 is synced only makes the caller's own settle revert at src/PoolManager.sol:360. Fees accrue at swap time (src/PoolManager.sol:238) and the swapper must still settle before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112). Passed to the code units as a lead for a second reading.

cleared.check: Whether the CAS20 Asset multiplier rebases balanceOf at the PoolManager (A2).
cleared.result: Safe by specification. BEP-702 section 3.12 says balanceOf returns the raw unscaled balance and the multiplier changes only the scaled view functions. To be re-checked against the client after Jenner.

cleared.check: Whether EIP-7702 changes A7 on these chains compared with Ethereum.
cleared.result: No new hazard. Polygon and BNB Smart Chain have the same set-code transactions as Ethereum. Avalanche rejects them. A delegated account used as a hook gives its owner the same power as an upgradeable proxy hook, and permissions still come from the address bits (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:337-339).

cleared.check: Whether the hardcoded NanoBlackList can freeze the PoolManager today.
cleared.result: Not today. The list holds three addresses and the PoolManager is not among them. The check applies only to the top-level sender and recipient of a transaction, so calls that reach the PoolManager through a router would still execute. Adding an address needs a client release adopted by validators.

cleared.check: Whether Circle USDC treats the PoolManager differently on these chains than on Ethereum (A6).
cleared.result: Same control as on Ethereum. isBlacklisted(PoolManager) returned false on Polygon USDC 0x3c49…3359 and Avalanche USDC 0xB97E…8a6E. A blocklist entry would freeze every USDC pool, as it would on Ethereum.
cleared.source: rpc eth_call isBlacklisted(address) on both USDC contracts via the RPC URLs in networks.json, 2026-11-22

cleared.check: Whether the native asset precompiles at 0x0100…01 and 0x0100…02 can move AVAX or give AVAX a second token face.
cleared.result: Safe. Coreth v0.10.0 deprecated Native Asset Call and Native Asset Balance, and they concerned non-AVAX native tokens.

cleared.check: Whether BNB or AVAX has an ERC-20 alias at a system address like POL has on Polygon.
cleared.result: None found. The BSC system contract list has no token wrapper of the native balance, and WBNB and WAVAX are ordinary contracts with their own balances. The Avalanche precompile list was taken from documentation and release notes, not from client source.

leads.question: After Jenner activates on 2026-12-08, what does the client implementation of CAS20 return for transfer and balanceOf when called by the PoolManager, has the ActivationRegistry opened token creation, and which CAS20 tokens have pools?
leads.why: The finding on CAS20 rests on a Draft BEP. Return data shape, static call behaviour and gas metering decide whether sync, settle and take work at all with these tokens.

leads.question: Can any sequence of hook callbacks, token callbacks or ERC-6909 operations profit from calling the fee adapter's collect while the PoolManager is unlocked, given that collectProtocolFees in src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57 never checks the lock?
leads.why: Fee collection is reachable by any address on Polygon and BNB Smart Chain and moves tokens out of the shared balance in the middle of an unlock. This unit found no gain but did not read Pool.sol in full.

leads.question: What does the StateReceiver code installed by Uburu at 0x1001 do differently, and can a failed state sync addressed to the governance proxy 0x8a1b…2374 be replayed later by anyone?
leads.why: A replayed old governance message could restore a protocol fee controller that governance has since replaced.

leads.question: How does Bor's BlockSTM executor handle transient storage and the serial fallback added in v2.11.0, and is the result identical to serial execution for transactions that share PoolManager transient slots?
leads.why: A divergence would break A1 for every transaction that touches the PoolManager.

leads.question: In the Continuous Execution VM source, is transient storage reset for every transaction, and do end-of-block operations such as atomic transactions ever call EVM code?
leads.why: This unit relied on documentation for A1 and for the absence of system callers on Avalanche since Helicon.

leads.question: If ACP-209 is scheduled, how do reserved balances and delegated accounts interact with hooks and with native transfers from the PoolManager?
leads.why: ACP-209 adds set-code accounts and a new precompile that holds part of an account's AVAX outside its normal balance.

leads.question: Who controls minting, upgrades or freezes of BSC-USD (0x55d3…7955), Binance-Peg USDC (0x8AC7…580d) and USD1 (0x8d0D…8B0d), which together make up most of the PoolManager's holdings on BNB Smart Chain?
leads.why: Issuer powers over these tokens were not read. A freeze or balance change at the PoolManager address stops or drains every pool that holds them.

leads.question: Who can mint or upgrade PoS-bridged tokens such as WETH 0x7ceB…f619 through state sync deposits and proxy admin rights?
leads.why: The PoolManager held 344 bridged WETH. Unbacked mints sold into pools would drain the counter-assets.

leads.question: What does the verified source of the Uniswap Wormhole message receiver enforce for emitter, sequence, timeout and target chain, and which Wormhole core contract and guardian set index does it read?
leads.why: The owner path finding inferred these checks from bytecode strings.

leads.question: Who can release assets from the token jar 0xc6ae6373cecc9e595a6c8b9fe581925a8c84f70a that receives protocol fees on Polygon and BNB Smart Chain?
leads.why: Anyone can move accrued protocol fees from the PoolManager into the jar, so the jar's release rule decides who ends up with them.

leads.question: lib/solmate is an empty directory in this checkout. Which Owned.sol will the CTF build compile against, and does its transfer function match what ProtocolFees.sol expects?
leads.why: The onlyOwner modifier at src/ProtocolFees.sol:29 cannot be reviewed from the repository as it stands.
